name: Romu family PRNGs (RomuDuoJr, RomuTrio, RomuQuad; C++ code and benchmark in t-mat gist)
baseline: PCG32 and xoroshiro128+ (same table also lists Wyrand, Shioi128, Sfc64, Stc64 and an Mmix control)
workload: Synthetic loop (as extracted from the gist): 1024 tests of 2,097,152 loop iterations each, five random values consumed and combined with arithmetic per iteration; throughput reported in GiB/s of generated random bits.
claimed_speedup: GCC 11.2.0 on Ubuntu: RomuDuoJr 11.40 GiB/s, RomuQuad 9.68, RomuTrio 9.29, RomuDuo 8.67 (64-bit outputs) versus Xoroshiro128p 8.02 GiB/s and Pcg32 3.71 GiB/s (32-bit outputs); Wyrand 8.85, Shioi128 10.15, Sfc64 9.22, Stc64 11.09, Mmix control 7.22. RomuDuoJr is about 1.42x Xoroshiro128p (derived from page data: 11.40/8.02).
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -fno-unroll-loops -fno-move-loop-invariants, GCC 11.2.0 on Ubuntu; an MSVC 19.32.31329 (x86) table is also in the gist, flags not extracted
tradeoffs: Romu is a non-linear generator: the period is seed dependent and probabilistic (the hasenbanck/romu README quotes the author's formula for the chance of a too-short cycle), there is no jump-ahead or stream support, and the rhet_RNG README notes the first 12 to 18 outputs of chaotic generators are low quality until warmed up. Not cryptographic.
caveats: Independent but casual single-author benchmark: code, compiler and flags are public, but no CPU model is stated, so it falls short of tier A. Pcg32 returns 32 bits per call while the Romu variants return 64, so GiB/s mixes output widths. No std::mt19937 row. The gist carries no license of its own: the Romu header credits Mark A. Overton (license not confirmed, romu-random.org and the paper arXiv 2002.11331 are unreachable here), the Wyrand code is marked Unlicense and the xoroshiro code credits Blackman and Vigna, so treat as reference. Last gist activity 2022-11-24. Related, not used for the tier: Almightygir/rhet_RNG (https://github.com/Almightygir/rhet_RNG) reproduces a 47 PRNG by 9 console 'Battle Royale' in which Romu2jr won, but the benchmark code is private and results are chart images only.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch 'fast PRNG faster than xoshiro PCG benchmark' (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) returned a comment saying the romu family is faster than multiply-add LCGs without failing TestU01/PractRand (thread id not identified, thread not openable); then WebSearch 'Romu random number generators fast nonlinear PRNG romuduojr github' (news.ycombinator.com + github.com) surfaced the gist.

name: vpxyz/xorshift (Go xorshift*, xorshift+, xoroshiro and splitmix64 generators)
baseline: Go math/rand (rand.NewSource Int63 source, and rand.New(source).ExpFloat64())
workload: go test -bench: nanoseconds per call of a raw Uint64 from each source versus rand.NewSource(...).Int63, and per rand.New(source).ExpFloat64() call for the wrapped variants.
claimed_speedup: Raw source ns/op: math/rand BenchmarkRandSource 4.93 versus XorShift128Plus 2.42, XorShift1024Star 2.40, Xoroshiro128Plus 2.66, Xoroshiro256PlusPlus 3.86, Xoroshiro256StarStar 3.93, SplitMix64 1.61. Wrapped in rand.Rand (ExpFloat64): BenchmarkRand 10.2 versus XorShift128Plus 8.42, Xoroshiro128Plus 8.10, SplitMix64 8.66. About 2.0x faster raw for XorShift128Plus and 3.1x for SplitMix64, but only 1.2x once wrapped in rand.Rand (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.14, go test -bench=. with default flags; benchmark code is xorshift_test.go in the repo (includes the math/rand baseline)
tradeoffs: Generators are not concurrency-safe (README says to wrap with a monitor goroutine). Generators with state larger than 64 bits are seeded via SplitMix64 as Vigna suggests. Implements Vigna's generators, so it carries their known linearity weaknesses in low bits for the + scramblers.
caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. Numbers are from 2020 on a 2012-era laptop CPU with Go 1.14, run by the repo author. The baseline is Go's default math/rand source, not a C++ standard facility. The wrapped rows call ExpFloat64 on both sides, so most of the raw gain is hidden by the distribution code. Go's standard library has since added math/rand/v2 (PCG, ChaCha8), so the gap against current Go is likely smaller (background knowledge, not tested).
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search (my 10-query WebSearch budget was spent on HN-domain queries that returned only already-catalogued projects); found on the GitHub topics page https://github.com/topics/xorshift, then opened the README, benchmark file and commits page.

name: pure-rand (fast-check PRNG library for JavaScript/TypeScript)
baseline: JavaScript native Math.random() (Xorshift128+ in Node 16.19.1) and the seedrandom, random-js, chance and faker Mersenne Twister libraries
workload: Shuffle of an array of 1,000,000 items; mean time in ms, with separate non-uniform and uniform (unbiased range) sections.
claimed_speedup: Non-uniform: pure-rand Xoroshiro128+ 24.5 ms versus native Math.random 33.3 ms (native 1.4x slower), seedrandom Xorshift128 28.8 ms (1.2x slower), seedrandom Alea 28.1 ms (1.1x slower), chance Mersenne Twister 142.9 ms (5.8x slower), faker Mersenne Twister 109.1 ms (4.5x slower). Uniform: pure-rand 53.5 ms versus random-js Mersenne Twister 119.6 ms (2.2x slower).
compiler_and_flags: Node 16.19.1, pure-rand 6.0.0, no flags; benchmark script perf/compare.cjs linked by permalink from COMPARISON.md (opened: shuffles 1,000,000 integers across the compared libraries)
hardware: 2 x x64 Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL @ 2.60GHz on GitHub Actions default runners, Ubuntu 22.04 container, 5.88 GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 117 stars; the PRNG behind fast-check (usage claim not checked)
tradeoffs: Pure functional API: generators are immutable and return a new generator on every call, which costs allocation but enables rollback and purity. Offers congruential32, Mersenne Twister, xorshift128+ and xoroshiro128+ with built-in unbiased uniform ranges and jump support.
caveats: JavaScript only, not usable from C++. Measured on shared GitHub Actions runners (noisy), with old versions (pure-rand 6.0.0, Node 16). The workload is a shuffle, so it measures range reduction as well as the generator. The native Math.random baseline appears only in the non-uniform section. Run by the project author. Congruential32 is listed as 1.1x faster than the recommended Xoroshiro128+ in the same table.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search; recalled from prior knowledge of JavaScript PRNG libraries because HN-domain searches only returned already-catalogued projects. Opened README, COMPARISON.md, the benchmark permalink and the commits page on github.com.

name: valyala/fastrand (Go scalable per-CPU pseudorandom generator)
baseline: Go math/rand (global rand.Int31n and rand.New(...) instances)
workload: go test -bench ns/op for Uint32n, per-goroutine RNG.Uint32n and math/rand Int31n at GOMAXPROCS=1, 2 and 4.
claimed_speedup: README: fastrand.Uint32n 29.7, 17.6 and 14.2 ns/op versus math/rand Int31n 31.8, 51.2 and 145 ns/op at GOMAXPROCS=1, 2, 4; per-goroutine RNG.Uint32n 6.50 ns/op versus rand.New(...).Int31n 17.9 ns/op at GOMAXPROCS=1. README text: comparable at one CPU, 3x faster at two CPUs and 10x faster at four CPUs.
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. with GOMAXPROCS set; Go version not stated
tradeoffs: Not cryptographically secure. Scaling comes from a sync.Pool of per-P generators, so the global functions are not a single reproducible stream; the README's own TODO says real per-CPU generators are still to be done.
caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. README lists benchmark output with no CPU model or Go version. The win is almost entirely about lock contention in Go's global math/rand of that era; later Go releases changed the global generator (background knowledge, not verified here), so the scaling gap may be outdated. Single-CPU gain over math/rand is small.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search; recalled from prior knowledge of Go RNG packages after HN-domain searches returned only catalogued projects. Opened repo page, README, source listing and commits page on github.com.

name: frand (lukechampine/frand, Go userspace CSPRNG)
baseline: Go crypto/rand (and math/rand in parallel benchmarks)
workload: Generating large amounts of random data, sequentially and in parallel.
claimed_speedup: README prose: 20x faster than crypto/rand when generating large amounts of random data, and over 100x faster when generating data in parallel; as fast and convenient as math/rand. No table or numbers beyond these ratios.
tradeoffs: Userspace CSPRNG seeded once from the kernel CSPRNG with no new entropy mixed in afterwards (README); the state lives in process memory, which the README acknowledges is easier for an attacker with memory access to read. Scales across cores through a sync.Pool of derived generators.
caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. First-party prose with no benchmark code in the repo listing and no hardware or Go version. Since commit 'switch to stdlib ChaCha8 generator' (2024-10-07) it is a thin wrapper over Go's math/rand/v2 ChaCha8, so the speedup really belongs to Go's stdlib ChaCha8 over crypto/rand rather than to this package's own code. Not a like-for-like comparison with PCG or xoshiro.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search (HN item 40087206 'Modern CSPRNGs can generate numbers at GB/s...' appeared in the results of the 'fast PRNG faster than xoshiro PCG benchmark' search and motivated looking at userspace CSPRNGs; thread not openable); recalled from prior knowledge. Opened repo page, README and commits page on github.com.

name: tinyrand (obsidiandynamics/tinyrand, Rust no_std PRNGs)
baseline: Rust rand crate (ChaCha12 StdRng) and the fastrand crate (Wyrand)
workload: README bandwidth table in GB/s for generating random numbers with each crate and algorithm.
claimed_speedup: rand ChaCha12 2.4 GB/s; tinyrand SplitMix 6.5; tinyrand Xorshift 6.7; fastrand Wyrand 7.5; tinyrand Wyrand 14.6. README TL;DR: tinyrand is 2x faster than fastrand and 6x faster than rand.
tradeoffs: no_std and heap-free, suitable for microcontrollers; ships Xorshift, SplitMix and Wyrand only; not cryptographically secure; README includes its own statistical test suite and Dieharder results.
caveats: Rust only, not callable from C++. README gives no CPU, compiler, flags or benchmark command, and the numbers are undated. The 6x figure compares a non-cryptographic PRNG with rand's ChaCha12 CSPRNG, which is not like-for-like; the like-for-like gap is 14.6 versus 7.5 GB/s for Wyrand (2x). The README mentions synthetic benchmarks in CI but the table itself has no linked source.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search; recalled from prior knowledge of Rust PRNG crates. Opened README, repo page and commits page on github.com.

name: mir-random (libmir/mir-random, D random number generators)
baseline: D Phobos std.random (Mt19937 generation and initialization, modulo-reduction bounded integers)
workload: README 'Comparison with Phobos' bullets: Mt19937 generation and initialization speed, and randIndex bounded-integer throughput using Lemire's fast alternative to modulo reduction.
claimed_speedup: Mt19937: +100% performance for initialization and +54% for generation versus Phobos (merged back to Phobos). randIndex with Lemire's method on x86-64 with LDC 1.6.0: 1.40x for uint with Mt19937_64, 1.73x for uint with Xoroshiro128Plus, 2.36x for ulong with Mt19937_64, 4.25x for ulong with Xoroshiro128Plus.
tradeoffs: D language with a Better C mode and no DRuntime dependency; provides Mt19937, PCG (Apache-2.0), SplitMix, XorshiftStar, Xoroshiro128Plus and Xoshiro256** engines plus ndslice-based random arrays and distributions; the new API uses opCall rather than a range interface. Not for cryptography.
caveats: D only, not callable from C++ without bindings. First-party bullets without a benchmark source or CPU, from the LDC 1.6.0 era (about 2017-2018). The Mt19937 improvements were merged back into Phobos, so that gap has probably closed. The 1.40x to 4.25x figures compare Lemire's reduction against modulo reduction on the same engine, not mir-random against another library. License per dub.sdl: BSL-1.0 by default, Apache-2.0 for PCG.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search; recalled from prior knowledge of non-C++ RNG libraries. Opened README, repo page and commits page on github.com, and read dub.sdl via raw.githubusercontent.com for the license.

name: xrandom (rtmigo/xrandom_dart, Dart random number generators)
workload: Time in milliseconds for nextInt, nextDouble and nextBool calls (iteration count not stated), AOT-compiled binaries.
claimed_speedup: Xrandom 627 / 640 / 391 ms versus dart:math Random 895 / 929 / 662 ms for nextInt / nextDouble / nextBool; about 1.43x, 1.45x and 1.69x faster (derived from page data). Qrandom/Drandom 933 / 1219 / 398 and Xoshiro256pp 1138 / 1182 / 406 are slower than Random for nextInt and nextDouble.
compiler_and_flags: Dart AOT-compiled binaries, flags and SDK version not stated
tradeoffs: Priority is bit-identical output across platforms (VM and JS), checked against C++ reference outputs; offers Xorshift, Xoshiro, Splitmix64 and Mulberry32 variants with the same API as dart:math Random; some generators are slower than the standard Random.
caveats: Dart only, not callable from C++. Benchmark code is not visible in the repo's top-level listing (lib, test, example, .github), so it is first-party numbers with partial methodology (hardware yes, SDK and iteration count no). The last visible commit is a bot merge from 2022-03-15. Only some of the shipped generators beat the baseline.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search; found on the GitHub topics page https://github.com/topics/xoshiro, then opened the README, repo page and commits page.

name: ZigguratGaussian (cicirello/ZigguratGaussian, Java ziggurat normal generator)
baseline: Java built-in Random.nextGaussian and ThreadLocalRandom.nextGaussian (polar method)
workload: JMH average time per Gaussian sample on JDK 17 for Random, ThreadLocalRandom and SplittableRandom, built-in versus the library's ziggurat.
claimed_speedup: results17.txt (JMH, ns/op): Random 103.037 built-in versus 17.393 ziggurat; ThreadLocalRandom 88.774 built-in versus 10.901 ziggurat; SplittableRandom 8.927 built-in versus 10.089 ziggurat (built-in faster). About 5.9x and 8.1x faster for Random and ThreadLocalRandom (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: JMH 1.37, OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM 17.0.2+8, no VM options, 5 warmup and 5 measurement iterations of 10 s, 1 thread; source and Maven build in experiment/timing17
stars_or_usage: 10 stars; published on Maven Central as org.cicirello:ziggurat
tradeoffs: Java port of the GSL C ziggurat implementation (GPL), with Java-specific optimizations. In Java 17 and later SplittableRandom already uses a ziggurat, so the library helps only for Random, SecureRandom and ThreadLocalRandom there. The author has folded it into the rho-mu library, which needs Java 25.
caveats: Java, not callable from C++; the gain is against Java's slow polar method rather than a C++ facility. Benchmark code and raw JMH output are public, but no CPU model is given (JDK path in the output suggests Windows), so it stays tier C; the accompanying arXiv report 2405.19493 was not opened (arXiv blocked). License file is GPL v3, SPDX variant (only vs or-later) not checked. HN-domain search snippet of the paper quotes 83% and 87% speedups; not verified.
found_via: Hacker News-domain WebSearch 'fast random sampling weighted alias shuffle ziggurat normal distribution library faster' listed the arXiv paper 2405.19493; the repo was then found on the GitHub topics page https://github.com/topics/ziggurat and opened with its experiment directory.

name: wrs (lorenzhs/wrs, parallel weighted random sampling and alias tables, ESA 2019)
baseline: GNU Scientific Library (GSL) alias table implementation
workload: Weighted random sampling: alias table construction and queries, sequential and parallel, versus GSL; benchmark scripts for an Intel 80-core and an AMD 32-core machine.
claimed_speedup: Numbers not seen on an opened page. WebSearch snippet only (attributed to the paper, arXiv 1903.00227, which could not be opened): alias queries more than 3x faster than GSL 2.5 and Vose-method table construction 30% faster than GSL.
compiler_and_flags: C++17 compiler, CMake 3.9.2 or later; optional Intel MKL for faster random variates, libnuma, and GSL for the comparison; flags not stated in README
hardware: Intel machine with 80 cores and 160 threads, and AMD machine with 32 cores and 64 threads (models not named in README)

Peer-reviewed at ESA 2019 and benchmark scripts are public (benchmark/ directory), hence tier B, but compiler flags and CPU models are not given. Baseline is GSL rather than a C++ standard facility such as std::discrete_distribution. Last commit is the dissertation version, 2020-12-09.

name: miranda (coolbutuseless/miranda, R package with C PRNGs: romu trio, xoshiro256+, lehmer64, splitmix64)
workload: bench::mark of generating 1 million uniform random numbers with each package function versus runif(N).
claimed_speedup: README text: these PRNGs are up to 20x faster than the built-in PRNGs in R, about 20x at best versus runif(); the timing chart is an image and the page text has no ns or ms values.
tradeoffs: R package with C source in src/, lifecycle marked experimental; includes jump-ahead for xoshiro256+; romu trio has a probabilistic period and xoshiro256+ has weak low bits; all four generators are listed as passing or having no systematic failures in BigCrush.
caveats: R package, usable from C++ only by reusing its small C sources. Chart image not readable, so the 20x figure is first-party text without per-generator numbers; no CPU, R version or compiler stated. The speedup includes R call and vector-allocation overhead of runif, so it is not a generator-only comparison, and the baseline is not std::mt19937 or PCG.
found_via: Lead from a README saved in the scratchpad by an earlier attempt at this assignment (not found by me through an HN search); I then opened the repo page and commits page on github.com.

name: Cromulent-PRNG (seanwevans/Cromulent-PRNG, cromulent128 with AVX2 variant)
baseline: xoshiro256, pcg64 and splitmix64 (in the repo's own bench_micro)
workload: bench_micro, 10,000,000,000 samples with seed 69420, ns per sample.
claimed_speedup: README sample output: xoshiro256 4.00 ns/sample, cromulent128 2.93, pcg64 1.76, splitmix64 1.27. cromulent128 is about 1.37x faster than xoshiro256 (derived from page data: 4.00/2.93) but about 1.7x slower than pcg64 and 2.3x slower than splitmix64.

The README says 'a modern CPU' with no model, no flags and 'exact numbers will vary'. Young repo (earliest commit on the first history page is 2026-07-01) with no stars. Kept as a flagged entry; the AVX2 variant is not benchmarked in the README.
